system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2185-08-18 20:21:00 to 2185-08-26 15:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with a history of cholangiocarcinoma and multiple biliary drains, was admitted with a low-grade fever and abnormal green-yellow discharge from his PTBD and percutaneous cholecystostomy tubes. He reported tenderness at the drain sites and mild nausea but denied vomiting or abdominal pain. Initial labs showed no leukocytosis or liver enzyme elevation, and blood cultures remained negative. He was started on IV meropenem for possible biliary infection but was afebrile upon admission. Interventional radiology performed a successful exchange of both the PTBD and cholecystostomy tubes, revealing a blocked PTBD that was cleared with balloon sweeping. Post-procedure, he remained stable, afebrile, and asymptomatic. A staging CT scan showed no progression of cholangiocarcinoma, stable biliary dilation, and no new metastatic lesions. Antibiotics were discontinued, and he was discharged home with instructions to monitor for fever, pain, or drain changes, and to follow up on rising alkaline phosphatase levels.
problems: Other mechanical complication of bile duct prosthesis, initial encounter
Migraine, unspecified, not intractable, without status migrainosus
Benign prostatic hyperplasia without lower urinary tract symptoms

# Fevers
# Cholangitis: Presented with fever, nausea, vomiting and MRCP 
findings of multifocal cholangitis with partial CBD stent 
obstruction. The patient was started on meopenem given his 
history of MDR E.coli. He was taken to ERCP but the procedure 
aborted before source control could be obtained due to hemobilia 
(see above). Transaminases downtrended and tbili remained 
stable. Blood cultures remained negative.  He remained afebrile 
and completed a 7-day course of meropenem without complication, 
relapse/recurrence of fever.

# Pancytopenia - anemia at baseline, stable. He has chronic 
thrombocytopenia which remained stable. He may also have an 
element of anemia of chronic disease.
Anaplasma PCR negative. Leukopenia was thought to be most likely

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  CHEST (PA AND LAT)

INDICATION:  History: ___ with fever// evaluate for infection

TECHNIQUE:  Chest PA and lateral

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph ___, CT chest ___

FINDINGS: 

Cardiac silhouette size is normal.  Mediastinal and hilar contours are within
normal limits.  The pulmonary vasculature is not engorged.  Lungs are clear
without focal consolidation.  No pleural effusion or pneumothorax is seen. 
Calcified granuloma within the right upper lobe is unchanged.  Embolization
coils are seen in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen.  There are mild
degenerative changes noted in the thoracic spine.  Biliary stents are
incompletely visualized in the upper abdomen.

IMPRESSION: 

No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.

EXAMINATION:  LIVER OR GALLBLADDER US (SINGLE ORGAN)

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with a history of cholangiocarcinoma and prior
PTBD who is admitted with fevers and a new transaminits.// Evaluate for cause
of fevers and transaminitis.

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the abdomen were
obtained.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal ultrasound ___

FINDINGS: 

LIVER: The hepatic parenchyma appears mildly coarsened.  The atrophic left
lobe is not well seen.  The contour of the liver is smooth. There is no focal
liver mass. The main portal vein is patent with hepatopetal flow. There is no
ascites.

BILE DUCTS: There is no intrahepatic biliary dilation. The CHD measures 5 mm.

GALLBLADDER: Poorly visualized.  Of note, the patient recently ate.

PANCREAS: The imaged portion of the pancreas appears within normal limits,
without masses or pancreatic ductal dilation, with portions of the pancreatic
tail obscured by overlying bowel gas.

SPLEEN: Enlarged, measuring 16.7 cm in length.

KIDNEYS: The left kidney measures 12.9 cm in length.  The right kidney
measures 11.1 cm in length.  Survey images of both kidneys demonstrate no
hydronephrosis.

RETROPERITONEUM:  The visualized portions of aorta and IVC are within normal
limits.

IMPRESSION:


1. Mildly coarsened hepatic parenchyma with an atrophic left lobe which is not
well seen.
2. Stable splenomegaly.

EXAMINATION:  MRCP

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with cholangiocarcinoma ___ CRT ___ with
recurrent biliary obstruction/cholangitis ___ PTBD (drain fell out ___.
Presents with fevers, transaminitis.// As requested by ERCP team: Eval for
liver abscess, eval for evidence of any cholangitis

TECHNIQUE:  T1- and T2-weighted multiplanar images of the abdomen were
acquired in a 1.5 T magnet.
Intravenous contrast: 8 mL Gadavist.
Oral contrast:  1 cc of Gadavist mixed with 50 cc of water was administered
for oral contrast.

COMPARISON:  MRCP ___

FINDINGS: 

Lower Thorax: Limited evaluation of the lung bases are notable for
atelectasis.  No pleural effusion.

Liver: There are new multifocal areas of parenchymal restricted diffusion, T2
hyperintensity, and arterial hyperenhancement with biliary wall thickening and
peribiliary enhancement within the peripheral ducts of segments V and VI,
consistent with multifocal cholangitis (1201:67, 97).  Central ducts do not
show abnormal enhancement.  Intrahepatic right-sided bile ducts are only
mildly dilated with degree of dilation  unchanged since prior study. No
hepatic abscess.  No signal drop on out of phase imaging to suggest hepatic
steatosis.

Mild progression of left intrahepatic biliary duct dilation with unchanged
left hepatic lobe atrophy when compared to ___.  Again seen is a large
indeterminate T1 hypointense irregular area surrounding the two common bile
duct stents which demonstrate arterial hyper enhancement that persists on
delayed phase imaging and may represent posttreatment fibrosis however
residual tumor would be similar in appearance. There are additional smaller
foci small within this area that progressively enhance without arterial
hyperenhancement and are more consistent with atrophic posttreatment changes
(10:62; 1201:61).

Two common bile duct stents are noted. There is some debris in the stent
draining the left ducts superiorly which may be causing the upstream left duct
dilation given that the dilated ducts are patent up to the stent. Additionally
some debris within the inferior aspect of the right common bile duct stent is
noted (10:71, 93).

Pancreas: Diffuse pancreatic atrophy with mild dilation of the main pancreatic
duct is unchanged. Unchanged 0.4 cm pancreatic body cystic lesion is most
likely a side branch IPMN (4:22).

Spleen: 1.9 cm accessory spleen is noted.  Spleen is large measuring 16.1 cm. 
No focal lesion.

Adrenal Glands: Unremarkable.

Kidneys: Bilateral T2 hyperintense nonenhancing renal cysts are noted. 
Otherwise unremarkable.  No hydronephrosis.  No perinephric fat stranding.

Gastrointestinal Tract:  Distal esophagus, stomach, visualized small and large
bowel are unremarkable.  No obstruction.

Lymph Nodes: No retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymph node enlargement.

Vasculature: Patent vasculature.  No abdominal aortic aneurysm.  Celiac axis,
SMA, bilateral renal arteries, and ___ are patent.  Hepatic anatomy is
conventional.  Hepatic veins are patent.  Main portal vein, SMV, and splenic
vein are patent.  Distal right portal vein is severely attenuated at its
bifurcation, unchanged since prior (1203:76).  The left portal vein is
severely diminutive throughout its course, unchanged since prior (1203:60).  
Small arterioportal fistula along the hepatic dome is noted (1201:29).
Osseous and Soft Tissue Structures: Unremarkable.


IMPRESSION:


1. Multifocal cholangitis predominately involving segments V and VI.  No
hepatic abscess.
2. Mild progression of left intrahepatic biliary duct dilation with persistent
atrophy of the left hepatic lobe.  Persistent areas of abnormal enhancement at
the biliary confluence likely related to posttreatment inflammatory fibrosis
however viable tumor cannot be excluded.  No new soft tissue lesion
identified.
3. Findings suspicious for partial obstruction of the stent draining the left
bile ducts which may be causing slight progression of upstream left biliary
duct dilation.
4. Unchanged severe attenuation of the right and left portal veins.

NOTIFICATION:   The findings were discussed with ___, M.D. by ___
___, M.D. on the telephone on ___ at 11:38 am, 5 minutes after
discovery of the findings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been having fevers. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had a fever for a few days now, along with nausea and vomiting. No belly pain though. I was worried because of my history with the bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your past cholangiocarcinoma and stents, we need to be careful. We’ll run some tests to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I remember last time it was a stent issue. Should we be worried about that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. We’ve ordered blood work and a chest X-ray to start. Your vitals look stable—no fast heart rate or low oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my blood pressure is okay? I’ve been on atenolol for migraines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your BP is 120 over 72—perfect. We’ll keep you on atenolol unless something changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray was clear, no pneumonia. We also did an ultrasound of your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver looks a bit coarse, and your left lobe is still atrophic. Your spleen is enlarged, but that’s been stable. No fluid or masses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But could this be related to the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your labs showed a high band count—13%—which suggests infection. We’re starting IV meropenem because of your history with resistant E. coli.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Meropenem again? That’s strong stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but given your past infections, we want to cover all bases. Blood cultures are negative so far, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled an MRCP today to get a better look at your bile ducts and stents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRCP is back. It shows multifocal cholangitis—so inflammation in several bile duct areas—especially on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. There’s also concern that your left stent might be partially blocked, which could be causing the inflammation upstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled an ERCP tomorrow to clean out the stent. The goal is to clear any debris and restore flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. They’re not fun, but I’ll do it if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. Also, your platelets are low—85—so we’ll watch for bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s been low for a while. Is it worse now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stable. Likely due to your chronic liver issues and past treatments. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. Johnson. The ERCP was partially successful. We cleared some debris from the left stent, but there was bleeding from the bile duct.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bleeding? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s called hemobilia. It’s rare but can happen after stent manipulation. The good news is it stopped on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No surgery needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your hemoglobin stayed stable, and you’re not tachycardic. We didn’t need a CT angiogram or embolization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. So the stent is clear now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partially. We cleared the left side, but the right stent wasn’t accessed due to the bleeding. We’ll monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile since yesterday. Liver enzymes are improving. We’ll continue meropenem for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today show your white count is trending down, and transaminases are improving. Still no growth in blood cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was likely the bile duct infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The cholangitis explains the fever and nausea. The antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? I’m usually diet-controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve you on sliding scale insulin while you’re here. Your glucose was 200 on admission—stress can raise it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll go back to diet after discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, unless your levels stay high. We’ll check again before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No fever, eating normally, and labs keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by Friday. We want to finish your antibiotic course and make sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bleeding? Should I watch for that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The risk is low now. If you notice black stools or feel lightheaded, call us. But it’s unlikely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the sixth day of antibiotics. You’ve had no fever, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So one more day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll discharge you tomorrow. We’ll review your meds and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to see my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The MRCP showed no new tumor, but the area near the stents is still suspicious. Your oncologist will decide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my stents—will I need another ERCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If symptoms return, we may need to address the right stent. But for now, you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day. You’ve completed your antibiotics, labs are good, and you’re feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume your usual meds—atenolol, tamsulosin, pantoprazole. Watch for fever, abdominal pain, or jaundice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get a fever again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER. It could mean another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your discharge summary is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just remember: follow up with your gastroenterologist and oncologist. And call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with a history of cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents, was admitted with fever, nausea, and vomiting. Workup revealed multifocal cholangitis and partial stent obstruction on MRCP. He was started on IV meropenem for suspected biliary infection. During ERCP to clear the stent, he developed hemobilia which resolved spontaneously without intervention. He remained hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and improved clinically. His pancytopenia remained stable throughout. He completed a 7-day course of antibiotics and was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up planned with gastroenterology and oncology.
